# Muhammad Usman Amin Siddiqi, PhD

<div class="hero-subtitle">Energy & Environmental Policy · Public Opinion · Behavioural Science</div>

<div class="hero-affiliation"><strong>Postdoctoral Research Associate</strong>, Department of Psychology, University of Bath<br><strong>Honorary Research Fellow</strong>, Centre for Energy Policy, University of Strathclyde</div>

<div class="hero-copy">I am an interdisciplinary social scientist studying how people understand, evaluate and respond to climate change, energy transitions, environmental risks and emerging energy technologies. My work connects public opinion and behavioural science with questions of policy design, social acceptance and the distribution of costs and benefits.</div>

<div class="section-label">Research focus</div>

## Social dimensions of climate and energy transitions

<p class="lede">My research asks a practical question: what makes climate and energy transitions not only technically possible, but also publicly acceptable, behaviourally realistic and socially responsive?</p>

::: {.card-grid}
::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">01</div>

### Energy transitions & public acceptance

Public perceptions of hydrogen, ammonia, offshore renewable energy and the infrastructure needed for low-carbon energy systems.
:::

::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">02</div>

### Climate risk & behaviour

How extreme weather, perceived harm, information and social interaction shape preparedness, climate action and policy support.
:::

::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">03</div>

### Public opinion & environmental policy

How knowledge, values, political and social identities, and perceived costs and benefits influence policy preferences.
:::
:::

::: {.band}
<div class="section-label">Current project</div>

## Ocean-REFuel: public acceptance of future energy systems

At the University of Bath, I contribute to **Ocean-REFuel**, an EPSRC-funded interdisciplinary programme examining the conversion of ocean renewable energy into zero-carbon hydrogen and ammonia fuels. My work focuses on public attitudes, acceptance, policy support and the social dimensions of emerging energy systems.

<a class="btn-academic" href="research.html#ocean-refuel">Current research →</a>
:::

## Recent publications

::: {.pub-list}
::: {.pub-card}
<div class="pub-meta">2026 · <em>npj Climate Action</em> · Open access</div>
<div class="pub-title">Seeing is believing or believing is seeing: divergent pathways to climate action and policy support following extreme weather events</div>
<div class="pub-meta"><span class="my-name">Siddiqi, M. U. A.</span>, Giordono, L., Peterson, H. L., Zanocco, C., Stelmach, G., Flora, J., & Boudet, H.</div>
<div class="pub-actions">
<details class="paper-details"><summary>About the paper</summary><div class="paper-summary">The paper is organised around a central question: Does experiencing extreme weather change how people think and act about climate change, or do their existing beliefs shape how they interpret those experiences? 

Some social science theory suggests that personal exposure to such events gives rise to beliefs that spur climate change actions and/or policy support (“seeing is believing”). Alternative theory suggests that beliefs about climate change instead shape event interpretation (“believing is seeing”), attenuating responses for non-believers. Research about how extreme weather events influence actions and policy preferences is inconclusive and sometimes contradictory. 

Using data from communities affected by wildfires in Oregon and hurricanes in Alabama, we employed Structural Equation Modelling to examine how extreme-weather experiences, climate concerns, and social norms relate to individual actions and support for climate mitigation and adaptation policies.

We show that there is no single pathway from experiencing an extreme event to climate action. What people experience, and what they see others around them doing, matters for individual preparedness and community helping behaviors. However, support for climate policies is more strongly tied to what people already believe, their political orientations, and how they interpret the event.

Experiencing a wildfire or hurricane can make risk immediate and personal, so taking steps to protect yourself can be a fairly direct response to that experience. Supporting broader policy change, however, requires connecting that experience to climate change as an underlying, collective cause; and that “connecting the dots” appears to be much more strongly filtered through prior beliefs and political orientations.</div></details>
<a class="pub-btn" href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s44168-026-00381-3">Read article ↗</a>
</div>
:::

::: {.pub-card}
<div class="pub-meta">2026 · <em>Energy Policy</em> · Open access</div>
<div class="pub-title">Community benefit agreement preferences for energy development offshore California, Oregon, and Washington: Insights from a choice-based conjoint experiment</div>
<div class="pub-meta">Taufiq, H. A., Stelmach, G., Rahman, U., <span class="my-name">Siddiqi, M. U. A.</span>, & Boudet, H.</div>
<div class="pub-actions">
<details class="paper-details"><summary>About the paper</summary><div class="paper-summary">The paper is organised around a central question: What should community benefits look like when offshore renewable energy development affects local communities? Community Benefit Agreements (CBAs) are increasingly used to ensure that communities hosting or affected by major energy projects share in their benefits. Yet we know surprisingly little about what the public actually wants these agreements to contain, how large the benefits should be, who should receive them, and who should manage the funds.

Using a survey of 2,999 residents of California, Oregon, and Washington, we conducted a choice-based conjoint experiment in which respondents chose between hypothetical CBAs that varied along three dimensions: the size of the benefit package, where the funds would be directed, and who would manage them. This allowed us to examine not only overall preferences, but also how people make trade-offs between different features of an agreement.

We find that larger benefit packages are generally preferred, but how the money is used matters as well. Respondents favoured investments in affordable housing and community services, such as healthcare, schools, and parks, over environmental restoration or payments directed to affected individuals. They also preferred CBA funds to be managed by established or newly created non-profit organisations rather than local governments. Importantly, there is no single CBA design that appeals equally to everyone. Preferences varied by age, income, education, residential location, and political ideology. 

The broader message is that a Community Benefit Agreement is not simply about offering more money. Its perceived value also depends on what communities believe the money should accomplish and which institutions they trust to manage it. Designing CBAs through meaningful local engagement, and adapting them to the social, economic, and geographic context of affected communities, may therefore be just as important as the overall size of the benefit package.</div></details>
<a class="pub-btn" href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0301421526002090">Read article ↗</a>
</div>
:::

::: {.pub-card}
<div class="pub-meta">2025 · <em>Environmental Policy and Governance</em> · Open access</div>
<div class="pub-title">Understanding public preferences for energy efficiency policies in building and agricultural sectors in the western US: Values, knowledge, and identity</div>
<div class="pub-meta"><span class="my-name">Siddiqi, M. U. A.</span>, & Wolters, E. A.</div>
<div class="pub-actions">
<details class="paper-details"><summary>About the paper</summary><div class="paper-summary">The paper is organised around a central question: What shapes public support for energy efficiency policies? Although energy efficiency can reduce energy use, emissions, and costs, realizing its potential depends partly on public support for policies that encourage or require more efficient practices. In the United States, environmental and energy policies are often viewed through a political lens, but we ask whether political ideology alone adequately explains these preferences, or whether environmental values, social identities, and knowledge also matter.

Using survey data from residents of California, Idaho, Oregon, and Washington, we examined support for two different approaches to energy efficiency: requiring high energy-efficiency standards for new construction and providing tax incentives for farmers to adopt more energy-efficient methods of producing and transporting food. We examined how support for these policies relates to demographics, political ideology, environmental values, social group identities, and policy knowledge.

We find broad public support for both policies, but the factors associated with that support extend well beyond the familiar liberal–conservative divide. The broader message is that public preferences for energy policy cannot be reduced to political ideology or a simple knowledge deficit. How people understand their relationship with the environment, whether they believe their actions can make a difference, and the social groups with which they identify can be at least as important—and in some cases more important—than how much they know about the policy itself. Building support for energy-efficiency policies may therefore require engaging with people's values and identities, rather than relying primarily on providing more technical information.</div></details>
<a class="pub-btn" href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/eet.2131">Read article ↗</a>
</div>
:::

::: {.pub-card}

<div class="pub-meta">
2023 · <em>Disasters</em> · 47(4), 1138–1172
</div>

<div class="pub-title">
Disaster preparedness and community helping behaviour in the wake of the 2020 Oregon wildfires
</div>

<div class="pub-meta">
<span class="my-name">Siddiqi, M. U. A.</span>, Giordono, L., Zanocco, C., Stelmach, G., Flora, J., & Boudet, H.
</div>

<div class="pub-actions">

<details class="paper-details">
<summary>About the paper</summary>

<div class="paper-summary">
Using a survey administered after the 2020 Oregon wildfires, the study compares factors associated with household disaster preparedness and community helping. Greater harm, climate concern, information seeking, informal discussion, and perceived preparedness among others were associated with stronger behavioural responses.
</div>

</details>
